comps.title: Hardware Heroes Trading Cards
comps.summary: Year 8 design a collectable trading card for one computer component, with stats, a picture and a fact, linked to the Hardware & Software unit.
comps.brief: Every computer is a team of heroes working together. Choose one component (for example the CPU, RAM, hard drive, SSD, graphics card, motherboard, a sensor or a printer) and design a trading card for it. Give it a hero name, a picture you have drawn or made yourself, three power stats (such as speed, storage or energy use) and a short 'special move' that explains what it really does inside the computer. Great cards are accurate, easy to read across a corridor, and make people want to collect the whole set.

entry.help: Make your card on one PowerPoint or Google Slides slide set to portrait (File, Page setup). Use shapes and your own drawings or icons from the built-in Insert Icons tool, not pictures copied from the internet. Save it as a picture: in PowerPoint use File, Export, PNG; in Google Slides use File, Download, PNG image. Upload the PNG in the revision app. One card per pupil. Do not put your name on the card itself.

setup: Make a one-slide card template (title box, picture box, three stat bars, special move box) and post it on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app with a closing date two weeks after launch, category Silver.
Put a launch slide in Year 8 assembly or form-time notices: 'Which component is your hero?'
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch at the end of a Hardware & Software lesson: show two example cards (one good, one weak) and let the class decide which is more accurate.
Give pupils a list of components so the set covers input, output, processing and storage, and encourage different choices within a class.
Run a 10-minute 'fact check' starter the next lesson: pupils swap draft stats with a partner who checks one fact.
Remind the year group via Google Classroom three days before the deadline and again on the day.
Pupils without home access finish at the lunchtime sessions; accept entries up to the end of the closing day.
Close the competition in the app and judge within a week.
resources: PowerPoint or Google Slides on school accounts
List of components with short definitions
Colour printer for the display set

rubric.look: Top marks: the special move and stats correctly describe what the component does and how it compares. Low marks: wrong or vague facts.
Top marks: clear layout, readable fonts, sensible colours, works when printed. Low marks: cluttered or hard to read.
Top marks: own drawings or creative use of icons and a memorable hero name. Low marks: copied images or a generic idea.
Top marks: a Year 8 who has never heard of the part would understand it. Low marks: jargon left unexplained.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden, then a Year 13 pupil re-marks the top ten to moderate. Tie-break on Accuracy. About 60 entries take roughly 90 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus up to five Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Print the top 20 as a 'collect the set' corridor display outside the DT room.
Show winners in Year 8 assembly as a slideshow with first name, initial and house only.
Laminate the winning set as real cards to use in Hardware lessons next year.
Certificates for placed and Highly commended entries.
comps.curriculum: Y8 Hardware & Software (input, output, processing, storage), presentation skills; TransformED S9 (memory capacity and processing power), C5 (communication for a specified audience), E3 (crediting sources).
comps.extension: Design a 'team-up' card showing how two components work together, for example the CPU and RAM in the fetch-execute idea.
comps.safety: Use only your own drawings or built-in icons; no images copied from websites. No names or photos of pupils on the cards.

comps.title: Scratch Maze Escape
comps.summary: Year 8 build a short Scratch maze game with a timer or score and at least two levels.
comps.brief: Build a maze game in Scratch where the player has to escape before time runs out. Your game should have a player sprite controlled by the keyboard, walls that stop the player, a timer or score, and at least two levels. The best games have clear instructions, are fair but challenging, and have a little surprise, such as a key to collect or an enemy that patrols. Think about who will play it: a Year 8 at lunchtime who has never seen it before.

entry.help: Build your game in Scratch. If you have a Scratch account, click Share, then copy the project link from the address bar and paste it into the revision app. If you do not have an account, use the Scratch editor in school or the offline editor, choose File, Save to your computer, put the .sb3 file in your school OneDrive, share it as 'People in Enniskillen Royal Grammar School with the link can view' and paste that link. Do not put your full name in the project title or notes. One game per pupil or per pair.

comps.time: 3 weeks (1 lesson launch + homework and lunchtimes)
setup: Make a 'starter maze' Scratch project showing arrow-key movement and the 'if touching colour then move back' wall check, and post the link on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (link entries), category Silver, closing date three weeks after launch.
Announce it in Year 8 assembly with a 20-second clip of the starter maze.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch lesson: pupils remix the starter maze and add a timer variable in the first 20 minutes so everyone can enter something.
Show a short checklist: movement, walls, timer or score, two levels, instructions screen.
Lunchtime 'bug clinic' once a week for pupils stuck on levels or variables.
Check after week 2 that pupils without home accounts have saved their .sb3 to OneDrive.
Send reminders on Google Classroom three days before and on the closing day.
Close entries and play-test each game for two minutes when judging.
resources: School OneDrive for pupils without Scratch accounts

rubric.look: Top marks: clear goal, fair challenge, players want another go. Low marks: impossible or no real challenge.
Top marks: variables for timer or score, levels changed with broadcasts or costumes, tidy scripts. Low marks: only basic movement.
Top marks: instructions screen, clear win and lose messages, readable colours. Low marks: player has to guess what to do.
Top marks: an original twist such as keys, enemies or a story. Low marks: an unchanged copy of the starter.

comps.judging: Teacher plays every game with names hidden (entry links only), noting scores in the app. A People's Choice award is decided by Year 8 votes at the lunchtime arcade of the top eight, separate from house placings. Tie-break on Gameplay. About 60 games take around 2.5 hours, so judge over two sessions. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Lunchtime arcade in the DT room playing the top eight games on the class PCs.
Add the winners to a teacher-run Scratch studio linked from the department site (no pupil names in titles).
Show gameplay screenshots in Year 8 assembly with first name, initial and house.
Certificates for placed and Highly commended entries.
comps.curriculum: Y8 Scratch (sequence, selection, iteration, variables, broadcasts); TransformED C1 (user-centred design for games), S1 (plan, develop, test, refine), C4 (abstraction).
comps.extension: Add a high-score system using a list, or a level editor that lets the player draw their own maze.
comps.safety: Scratch is designed for ages 8 to 16. Pupils under 13 sharing online should use a parent-approved or teacher-created class account; otherwise submit through OneDrive. No real names, photos or personal details in projects. Use only Scratch library sprites, your own drawings or sounds you made.

comps.title: Tuck Shop Tycoon
comps.summary: Year 8 build a spreadsheet model to plan a sports-day tuck shop and show how price changes affect profit.
comps.brief: Your house has been asked to run a tuck shop at sports day, and you are the finance manager. Build a spreadsheet that lists at least six items with their cost price, selling price and how many you expect to sell, then calculates income, costs and profit using formulas. Add a chart and a 'what if' cell (for example a price change or a rainy day that halves sales) so you can show what happens. The best entries are accurate, clearly laid out and give a sensible recommendation about what to sell and at what price.

entry.help: Build your model in Excel or Google Sheets. Take one screenshot showing your table, chart and recommendation (on Windows press Windows + Shift + S; on a Chromebook press Ctrl + Shift + Show windows). Turn on formula view for a second screenshot if you can (Formulas, Show Formulas) and paste both into one slide or document, then save as a PNG. Upload the image in the revision app. One entry per pupil.

setup: Prepare a price list sheet (realistic cost prices for drinks, snacks and fruit) and post it on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Silver, closing a week before sports day.
Announce in form time: 'Can your house make the most money at sports day?'
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch in a spreadsheet lesson: demonstrate =B2*C2 and =SUM, then let pupils build the first three rows.
Mini-lesson on 'what if' cells: change one value and watch the model update.
Show how to make a column chart of profit per item.
Lunchtime help session for formulas and screenshots.
Remind pupils that the recommendation sentence counts for marks.
Close entries and judge before sports day so winners can be announced on the day.

rubric.look: Top marks: correct formulas for income, cost and profit that update automatically. Low marks: typed-in answers or errors.
Top marks: a clear variable that changes the outcome, with the effect explained. Low marks: no way to test a scenario.
Top marks: clear headings, currency format, a suitable labelled chart. Low marks: unlabelled or messy.
Top marks: a sensible, evidence-based decision using the numbers. Low marks: no conclusion.

comps.judging: Teacher judges screenshots with names hidden; check formula-view screenshots for the top ten. Tie-break on Modelling. About 60 entries take about 75 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Announce the winners on sports day or in the next Year 8 assembly.
Corridor display of the best charts with first name, initial and house.
If the school runs a real stall, invite the winner's recommendation to be used.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: Y8 spreadsheets (formulas, formatting, charts); TransformED S7 (models and changing variables), S4 (data types: currency, integer), C5 (presenting for an audience).
comps.extension: Add a break-even calculation or use conditional formatting to highlight items that lose money.
comps.safety: Use made-up figures only; no real pupil names or money records.

comps.title: Pixel Perfect House Mascots
comps.summary: Year 9 create a 32 by 32 pixel art mascot for their house animal and explain the colour depth and file size.
comps.brief: Design a pixel art mascot for your house: the Belmore Hare, Benaughlin Eagle, Cuilcagh Fox or Trien Stag. Your image must be 32 by 32 pixels and use no more than 16 colours, including your house colour. Underneath, write two or three sentences explaining how many bits each pixel needs for your number of colours and roughly how big the file would be uncompressed. Great entries are instantly recognisable, use shading well and get the maths right.

entry.help: Use Piskel in your browser (no account needed) or a 32 by 32 grid in PowerPoint or Sheets. In Piskel, click Export, PNG, and set the scale to 10 so it is easy to see. Put the PNG on a PowerPoint slide with your explanation of colour depth and file size underneath, then export the slide as PNG and upload it in the revision app. Do not put your name on the image. One entry per pupil.

setup: Prepare a slide showing a 32 by 32 grid, the four house colours and a worked colour-depth example (16 colours = 4 bits, so 32 x 32 x 4 = 4096 bits = 512 bytes).
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Launch in Year 9 assembly with a pixelated mystery animal to guess.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch in a Computer Graphics lesson: show bitmap vs vector, then pupils sketch on squared paper first.
Demonstrate Piskel's palette, mirror tool and export settings.
Short starter in the next lesson: calculate the file size of a 16 by 16, 4-colour image.
Lunchtime drop-in for pupils who want help or a computer.
Reminder on Google Classroom three days before close.
Close entries and judge within a week.

rubric.look: Top marks: recognisable animal, good use of shading and outline at low resolution. Low marks: unclear shapes.
Top marks: correct bits per pixel and file size with working shown. Low marks: missing or wrong.
Top marks: exactly 32 by 32 and 16 colours or fewer, house colour used. Low marks: rules ignored.
Top marks: a mascot with personality that would work on a badge or banner. Low marks: generic.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden; a Year 14 guest judge checks the maths on the top ten. Tie-break on Artwork. About 60 entries take about an hour. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Corridor display grouped by house, like a pixel-art gallery.
Assembly slideshow showing the winning mascot for each house.
Offer the winning designs (with permission) for house noticeboards.
Certificates for placed and Highly commended entries.
comps.curriculum: Y9 Computer Graphics (bitmap images, resolution, colour depth) and binary/data; TransformED S9 (binary representation), C4 (abstraction: simplifying an image).
comps.extension: Make a 4-frame animated version in Piskel and export it as a GIF, or compare the file size as PNG vs BMP and explain the difference.
comps.safety: Original artwork only; do not trace logos, game characters or images from the internet.

comps.title: Fermanagh One-Page Wonder
comps.summary: Year 9 hand-code a single HTML and CSS page that promotes a Fermanagh landmark to visiting pupils.
comps.brief: A school from abroad is visiting Fermanagh and needs a one-page guide. Choose a local landmark such as Enniskillen Castle, Marble Arch Caves, Devenish Island or Cuilcagh Boardwalk, and build a single web page about it using HTML and CSS you have typed yourself. Include headings, a list, a link, a table or a navigation bar, and at least one image with alt text. The best pages are well structured, accessible and attractive, and the code is tidy and indented.

entry.help: Write your page in Notepad++, VS Code or the editor you use in class, with your CSS inside a <style> tag so everything is in one file. Images must be your own photos of places (no people) or free-to-use images with a credit; link to them by web address. When finished, open the .html file in Notepad, press Ctrl + A then Ctrl + C, and paste the whole code into the revision app text box. Do not put your name on the page. One entry per pupil.

setup: Post a starter HTML file with the basic structure (doctype, head, body, style) on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (text entries), category Silver, closing three weeks after launch.
Make a one-slide checklist: structure, CSS, alt text, credits, indentation.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch in a Web Design lesson: pupils inspect a simple tourist page and list what makes it useful.
Mini-lessons on alt text and colour contrast, linking to accessibility.
Teach how to credit images from free-licence sites.
Lunchtime coding clinic for missing tags and CSS selectors.
Reminder three days before close: paste the whole file, not just part of it.
To judge, paste each entry into a new .html file and open it in a browser.
resources: List of free image sites that allow reuse

rubric.look: Top marks: valid structure, headings in order, lists, links and correctly nested tags. Low marks: missing or broken tags.
Top marks: consistent styling with selectors, classes and layout. Low marks: no CSS or inline styling only.
Top marks: meaningful alt text, good contrast, readable font sizes. Low marks: missing alt text or poor contrast.
Top marks: accurate, useful information written for visiting pupils, sources credited. Low marks: copied text or uncredited images.

comps.judging: Teacher views each page and its code with names hidden. A Year 13 guest judge checks the top ten in the browser. Tie-break on HTML structure. About 60 entries take around 2 hours. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Screenshots of the top pages on a corridor display about Fermanagh.
Show the winning pages live in Year 9 assembly.
With permission, host the winners on the department website with no pupil names.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: Y9 Web Design (HTML/CSS); TransformED S2 (hierarchy, patterns and syntax in markup), C1 (user needs), E5 (accessibility, WCAG), E3 (crediting sources).
comps.extension: Make the page responsive with a media query so it works on a phone.
comps.safety: No photos of people. Credit every image and use only ones with a free licence or your own landscape photos. No personal details on the page.

comps.title: micro:bit Sports Day Gadget
comps.summary: Year 9 program a micro:bit gadget for sports day, such as a reaction timer, step counter or race starter, and test it in the simulator.
comps.brief: Invent a micro:bit gadget that would help at sports day. It could be a race starter with a random countdown, a reaction timer, a step counter using the accelerometer, a score keeper for two houses, or something new. Your program must use at least one input (a button, shake or sensor) and at least one variable, and it should work in the MakeCode simulator. Great entries solve a real problem, are tested properly and are simple for anyone to use.

entry.help: Build your program in Microsoft MakeCode for micro:bit in your browser (no account needed). Click Share, then Share Project, and copy the link into the revision app. In the description box in the app, write two sentences: what your gadget does and how you tested it. One entry per pupil or per pair. You do not need a micro:bit at home: the on-screen simulator is enough.

setup: Check the class set of micro:bits and batteries are working for the launch lesson.
Open the competition in the revision app (link entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch and before sports day.
Prepare a slide of example gadgets and a simple test table (input, expected output, actual output).
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch lesson: pupils brainstorm sports day problems in pairs, then pick one to solve.
Show how to use the simulator so pupils can carry on at home without kit.
Lunchtime sessions to test on real micro:bits.
Reminder to paste the Share link, not the editor address.
Close entries; test the top ten on a real micro:bit.
If possible, let the winning gadget be used at sports day.
resources: Class set of micro:bits with battery packs

rubric.look: Top marks: solves a real sports day problem in a clear way. Low marks: no clear purpose.
Top marks: inputs, variables, selection and loops used sensibly; code is tidy. Low marks: a single simple block.
Top marks: describes tests with expected and actual results. Low marks: no testing mentioned.
Top marks: clear display messages, anyone could use it. Low marks: confusing to operate.

comps.judging: Teacher runs each project in the simulator with names hidden, then tests the top ten on a real micro:bit. Tie-break on Usefulness. About 60 entries take around 2 hours. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Use the winning gadget at sports day or the house event if practical.
Demo the top four in Year 9 assembly using the simulator on the big screen.
Short write-up with screenshots on the department website.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: Y9 Micro:bits (inputs, outputs, sensors, variables) and models and simulations; TransformED S7 (simulation to test ideas), S1 (develop and test), S4 (data types).
comps.extension: Use radio so two micro:bits communicate, for example a starter that signals a finish-line timer.
comps.safety: Use classroom micro:bits under supervision; no wearing gadgets during races. MakeCode share links are public, so no names in the project title.

comps.title: Dream Machine on a Budget
comps.summary: Year 10 spec a PC for a given user on a fixed budget in a spreadsheet and justify each component choice.
comps.brief: A client needs a new computer and has a budget of 700 pounds. Choose one client from the list (a gamer, a video editor, a primary school, or a grandparent who wants video calls) and spec a PC that suits them. Use a spreadsheet to list each component (CPU, RAM, storage, graphics, power supply, case, monitor), its key specification, its price and a one-line reason, with the total calculated by formula. The best builds stay within budget, match the client's needs and show you understand what each part does.

entry.help: Build your spec sheet in Excel or Google Sheets. Use current prices from a UK retailer and include a 'source' column. Take a screenshot showing the whole table, total and justification, paste it on a slide with a short paragraph explaining your two most important choices, then export the slide as PNG and upload it in the revision app. One entry per pupil.

setup: Write four short client profiles and post them on Google Classroom with a spreadsheet template.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Announce in Year 10 form time.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch in an Under the Hood lesson: compare two real adverts and decide which suits a gamer.
Mini-lesson on clock speed, cores, RAM size, SSD vs HDD and GPU memory.
Pupils check compatibility basics (CPU socket, power supply wattage) with a partner.
Lunchtime help for spreadsheets and component research.
Remind pupils prices change, so judges use the prices they quote.
Close entries and judge within a week.

rubric.look: Top marks: every choice clearly matches the client's needs. Low marks: overkill or unsuitable parts.
Top marks: justifications use correct terms such as cores, clock speed and capacity. Low marks: 'it is good' style reasons.
Top marks: within budget, totals by formula, sources listed. Low marks: over budget or hand-typed totals.
Top marks: clear, well formatted and easy to follow. Low marks: messy or incomplete.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden; an A level pupil acts as guest judge for the top ten to check compatibility. Tie-break on Suitability. About 60 entries take around 90 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Display the best build for each client type on the corridor.
Assembly slide: 'four clients, four winners'.
Use the winning sheets as exemplars in next year's Under the Hood lessons.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: Y10 Under the Hood (CPU, memory, storage, GPU), spreadsheets; TransformED S9 (performance depends on memory and processing), C1 (user needs), E6 (energy use, optional).
comps.extension: Add a column for power consumption and estimate yearly running cost and carbon impact.
comps.safety: Research only; pupils must not buy anything or create retailer accounts.

comps.title: One-Week GameMaker Game Jam
comps.summary: Year 10 make a small GameMaker game to a surprise theme in one week, then submit a screenshot and a shared link to the project.
comps.brief: Game jams are where real developers make a game in a short time to a surprise theme. When the theme is revealed, you have one week to make a small game in GameMaker that fits it. Keep it simple: one room or level that works well is better than five that are broken. Great entries fit the theme in a clever way, play smoothly, have clear instructions and feel finished.

entry.help: Make your game in GameMaker on a school PC (or at home if you already use it with your parent or guardian's permission). Export the project with File, Export Project, Local Package (.yyz), put it in your school OneDrive, share it as 'People in Enniskillen Royal Grammar School with the link can view', and paste the link in the revision app. If you cannot share a file, upload a screenshot of your game with a short description of the controls and goal instead. One entry per pupil or per pair.

comps.time: 1 week (theme revealed Monday, closes next Monday)
setup: Choose a secret theme (for example 'Only one button', 'Gravity', or 'It's alive').
Check GameMaker is installed and working on the DT room PCs.
Open the competition in the revision app (image-or-link entries), category Silver, closing one week after the reveal.
Announce the date of the theme reveal in Year 10 assembly to build excitement.
Book the DT room every lunchtime of jam week so everyone has access to GameMaker.
run: Reveal the theme at the start of a Game Design lesson; pupils spend 15 minutes sketching ideas on paper.
Encourage a scope check: what is the smallest version of your game that works?
Run lunchtime jam sessions every day of the week; most work will happen here.
Mid-week stand-up: each pair says in one sentence what works and what is next.
Remind pupils the day before close to export and share their project.
Close entries and run the top games on school PCs to judge.

rubric.look: Top marks: the theme shapes the gameplay in a clever way. Low marks: theme only mentioned in the title.
Top marks: smooth controls, clear goal, fair challenge, no game-breaking bugs. Low marks: unplayable or no goal.
Top marks: sensible use of events, variables and objects; well organised. Low marks: minimal logic.
Top marks: title screen, instructions, sound or feedback, feels finished. Low marks: player has to guess.

comps.judging: Teacher plays each game with names hidden. A People's Choice award is voted by pupils at a lunchtime arcade of the top eight, separate from house placings. Tie-break on Theme. About 40 to 60 games take around 2.5 hours across two sessions. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Lunchtime arcade of the finalists in the DT room.
Screenshot gallery on the corridor with the theme in big letters.
Show a short screen-recorded clip of the winning game in assembly.
Certificates and a 'Jam Champion' badge on the department website.
comps.curriculum: Y10 Game Design (GameMaker events, objects, variables); TransformED S1 (planning, development, testing, refinement), C1 and C2 (user-centred design and refining usability), C4 (abstraction).
comps.extension: Add a second level or a saved high score, then write a short post-jam review of what you would change.
comps.safety: Use GameMaker's built-in assets, your own art and sound, or assets with a free licence and a credit. No violent or inappropriate content. Follow GameMaker's account terms if using it at home.

comps.title: Fix This App: Accessible Redesign
comps.summary: Year 10 redesign a deliberately poor school-app screen so it meets accessibility and good UX principles, with annotations.
comps.brief: We have designed a terrible school app screen: tiny text, low contrast, confusing buttons and no labels. Your job is to redesign it so that everyone can use it, including people with visual impairments, dyslexia or motor difficulties. Produce a before and after mock-up and annotate at least five changes with the design principle or accessibility guideline behind each. The best entries are clean, consistent and clearly explain who each change helps.

entry.help: Use the 'bad screen' image from Google Classroom. Design your new screen in PowerPoint, Google Slides or Google Drawings at phone size. Put the before and after side by side on one slide with numbered annotations, then export it as PNG and upload it in the revision app. One entry per pupil.

setup: Create one deliberately bad app screen (for example a homework planner) and post it on Google Classroom.
Prepare a one-page guide to key accessibility points: contrast, text size, labels, touch target size, not relying on colour alone.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch in a UX/accessibility lesson: pupils list everything wrong with the bad screen in five minutes.
Show a free online contrast checker and how to use it.
Discuss who is excluded by each problem, linking to digital ethics.
Lunchtime help session.
Reminder three days before close.
Judge within a week.
resources: PowerPoint, Google Slides or Google Drawings

rubric.look: Top marks: good contrast, readable text, large touch targets, labels, no reliance on colour alone. Low marks: problems remain.
Top marks: clear hierarchy, consistent design, obvious next step for the user. Low marks: still confusing.
Top marks: at least five changes, each explained with a principle and who it helps. Low marks: no reasons given.
Top marks: looks professional and believable as an app. Low marks: unfinished.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden; invite the school's learning support coordinator or a Year 14 pupil as guest judge for the top ten. Tie-break on Accessibility. About 60 entries take around 90 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Before and after corridor display titled 'Design for everyone'.
Assembly slide comparing the bad screen with the winner.
Use winning designs as exemplars for GCSE design principles.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: Y10 UX/accessibility and digital ethics; TransformED E5 (accessibility guidelines, WCAG), C1 and C2 (user-centred design, refining usability), C3 (user stories).
comps.extension: Write three user stories ('As a ... I want ... so that ...') and show how your design meets each.
comps.safety: Use made-up content only; no real pupil names, timetables or photos in the mock-up.

comps.title: Cyber Escape Room
comps.summary: Year 11 teams solve a set of capture-the-flag style puzzles on ciphers, binary, phishing and passwords, submitting each flag as text.
comps.brief: You are locked in a cyber escape room and the only way out is to find six secret flags. Each puzzle tests a GCSE skill: cracking a Caesar cipher, converting binary and hexadecimal, spotting the warning signs in a phishing email, judging password strength, reading a network diagram and finding a hidden clue in a file's properties. Work as a team, record your answers and explain how you found each one. The winning team has the most correct flags, with clear working, in the fastest time.

entry.help: Type your team name (house plus a number, for example Trien 2) and then each flag on a new line, like FLAG1: ANSWER, followed by one sentence explaining how you found it. Paste it into the revision app. One entry per team. Teams of up to 4 from the same house.

comps.time: 1 lunchtime or 1 lesson (45 minutes), with a 1-week homework window for absentees
setup: Make six puzzles on paper or slides (Caesar cipher, binary to ASCII, hex colour code, phishing email, password ranking, image file properties) each with a one-word flag.
Print a puzzle pack per team, or put them on a Google Classroom post released at start time.
Open the competition in the revision app (text entries), category Silver.
Announce the date in Year 11 form time and ask pupils to form house teams.
run: Run it as a timed lesson or lunchtime event; give teams 40 minutes.
Offer one hint card per team (using a hint costs 2 marks).
Pupils absent on the day can attempt it at a later lunchtime within a week.
Collect entries in the app before the end of the session.
Go through the answers together at the end: this is also great revision.
resources: ASCII table and binary place-value sheet

rubric.look: 3 marks for each correct flag. No marks for a wrong flag.
1 mark per flag with a clear, correct explanation of the method.
Start at 6; lose 2 for each hint card used.

comps.judging: Answers are marked against the answer key by the teacher; team names show only house and number. Tie-break on earliest submission time in the app. About 15 team entries take 20 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended for the best explanations. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Leaderboard slide in Year 11 assembly by team and house.
Post the puzzles (not answers) on the department website for others to try.
Certificates for the winning teams.
Corridor display of 'how we cracked it' explanations.
comps.curriculum: GCSE Unit 1 cyber security (phishing, passwords, malware), Unit 4 data representation (binary, hexadecimal, ASCII).
comps.extension: Each team designs one new puzzle for next year's escape room with an answer key.
comps.safety: All puzzles are offline or teacher-made; no real hacking, no attempts to access school systems. Phishing examples must be fictional.

comps.title: C# Code Sprint
comps.summary: Year 11 solve five short C# console problems of increasing difficulty, checked against teacher test cases.
comps.brief: Five problems, two weeks, one leaderboard. Each problem asks you to write a short C# console program, starting easy (for example converting a mark to a grade) and getting harder (validating a password, searching an array, a simple menu system). Your code must pass the test cases provided and some hidden ones. The best entries pass every test, use sensible variable names and comments, and handle bad input without crashing.

entry.help: Write each solution in Visual Studio or the C# environment you use in class. Paste all your solutions into the revision app text box, with a comment line like // Problem 3 above each one. Make sure each program compiles. One entry per pupil.

setup: Write five problems with 3 visible test cases each and 2 hidden ones, and post the problem sheet on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (text entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Announce in a Unit 4 lesson.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch by solving Problem 1 together in the first 10 minutes so everyone has a start.
Remind pupils about input validation and try/catch or TryParse.
Lunchtime code clinic: help with errors, but not with the logic.
Reminder three days before close.
Close and run each solution against the visible and hidden tests.
resources: Visual Studio or school C# environment
Hidden test cases for the teacher

rubric.look: Up to 4 marks per problem: visible tests 2, hidden tests 2.
Top marks: invalid input handled without crashing. Low marks: crashes on bad input.
Top marks: meaningful names, indentation and helpful comments. Low marks: hard to follow.

comps.judging: Teacher runs the code with names hidden. A Year 13 or 14 pupil can help run test cases. Tie-break on Robustness, then earliest submission. About 50 entries take around 2.5 hours. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Leaderboard on the DT room screen.
Model solutions shared afterwards on Google Classroom as revision.
Assembly mention of the winners by first name, initial and house.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: GCSE Unit 4 C# programming (selection, iteration, arrays, validation, testing with normal, boundary and erroneous data).
comps.extension: Write your own Problem 6 with test cases for next year's sprint.
comps.safety: Work must be your own. Do not paste problems into AI tools; any code copied from elsewhere must be credited in a comment and will not earn marks.

comps.title: Fermanagh in Numbers
comps.summary: Year 11 turn an open data set about Northern Ireland into a clear, honest infographic with a spreadsheet chart.
comps.brief: Data tells stories, but only if it is presented honestly. Choose an open data set about Northern Ireland or Fermanagh (for example rainfall, population, tourism or road safety), clean it in a spreadsheet, and create an infographic that tells one clear story for a Year 9 audience. Include at least one chart made from your spreadsheet, a headline finding and the source of your data. Great entries are accurate, easy to understand and avoid misleading tricks such as cut-off axes.

entry.help: Download a data set from an official open data site (such as NISRA or the Met Office) and build your chart in Excel or Google Sheets. Make your infographic on one portrait slide in PowerPoint or Google Slides, including the data source. Export it as PNG and upload it in the revision app. One entry per pupil.

setup: Choose three suitable open data sets and post the links on Google Classroom to save time searching.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Prepare a slide of misleading chart examples to discuss.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch lesson: pupils spot what is wrong with three misleading charts.
Show sorting, filtering and choosing the right chart type in a spreadsheet.
Lunchtime help for data cleaning and chart formatting.
Reminder three days before close: include the data source.
Judge within a week.

rubric.look: Top marks: data cleaned, sorted or filtered appropriately, correct calculations. Low marks: raw data pasted in.
Top marks: right chart type, labelled axes starting sensibly, units and title. Low marks: misleading or unlabelled.
Top marks: one clear headline a Year 9 would understand. Low marks: no clear message.
Top marks: clean layout, source credited. Low marks: cluttered or no source.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden; a maths teacher or Year 14 pupil acts as guest judge for the top ten. Tie-break on Honest chart. About 50 entries take about an hour. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Corridor display 'Fermanagh in Numbers'.
Share winning infographics on the school website or social media (no pupil names).
Use the best as exemplars in Unit 1 spreadsheets and digital applications revision.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: GCSE Unit 1 spreadsheets (sorting, filtering, charts) and digital applications; data and information; ethics of presenting data.
comps.extension: Add a second chart that compares two variables and explain whether one causes the other.
comps.safety: Use public, anonymised open data only. Credit the source. No data about individual pupils.

comps.title: Algorithm Olympics
comps.summary: Year 12 design a flowchart or pseudocode solution to a sports-day scoring problem and prove it works with a trace table.
comps.brief: The house captains need an algorithm that takes the results of each sports day race and works out the house totals and the overall winner, dealing with draws and disqualifications. Design the solution as a flowchart or in pseudocode, then prove it works with a trace table using the test data provided, including normal, boundary and erroneous data. Great entries are correct, efficient and easy to follow, and handle every awkward case.

entry.help: Draw your flowchart or write your pseudocode neatly using draw.io, PowerPoint, Google Drawings or on paper. Add your trace table underneath. If on paper, take a clear, well-lit photo of the page only (no faces or names). Combine everything onto one image if you can and upload it in the revision app. One entry per pupil.

setup: Write the problem statement and a table of test data (including a draw and a disqualified runner).
Post it on Google Classroom with the CCEA flowchart symbols as a reminder.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch at the end of a Unit 4 lesson by reading the problem together.
Remind pupils about trace tables and the three types of test data.
Lunchtime drop-in for questions about the problem (not the solution).
Reminder three days before close.
Judge within a week and go through the model answer as revision.

rubric.look: Top marks: produces the right totals and winner for every test case including draws and disqualifications. Low marks: fails normal data.
Top marks: complete, accurate trace table covering normal, boundary and erroneous data. Low marks: missing or wrong.
Top marks: correct symbols or pseudocode conventions, meaningful names. Low marks: hard to follow.
Top marks: uses loops and arrays rather than repeated code. Low marks: long repetitive solution.

comps.judging: Teacher marks with names hidden; a Year 14 guest judge checks the top ten trace tables. Tie-break on Correctness. About 50 entries take around 90 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Display the winning flowchart outside the DT room.
Share the model solution on Google Classroom for revision.
Assembly mention with first name, initial and house.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: GCSE Unit 4 algorithms (flowcharts, pseudocode), testing (normal, boundary, erroneous data, trace tables), arrays.
comps.extension: Code the algorithm in C# and test it with the same data.
comps.safety: Photos must show only the page; no faces, names or other pupils' work.

comps.title: 90-Second Tech Explainer
comps.summary: Year 12 make a 90-second faceless explainer video or podcast on a Unit 1 topic that doubles as revision for others.
comps.brief: Pick a GCSE Unit 1 topic that people find hard, such as cloud computing, network topologies, encryption, the Data Protection Act or the Computer Misuse Act, and explain it in 90 seconds or less. Make a screen-recorded slideshow, animation or audio podcast: no faces on camera. Aim it at a Year 11 who is revising for the first time. The best explainers are accurate, memorable, use a good example, and stick to the time limit.

entry.help: Make your video with PowerPoint (Record, then Export as MP4) or another school-approved tool, or record an audio podcast. Do not show your face or say your full name. Save the file in your school OneDrive, share it as 'People in Enniskillen Royal Grammar School with the link can view', and paste the link in the revision app. Maximum 90 seconds. Use only music and images you made or that are free to use, and credit them on the last slide. One entry per pupil or pair.

setup: Post a list of eligible Unit 1 topics on Google Classroom so entries cover a range.
Prepare a one-slide guide to recording in PowerPoint and sharing from OneDrive.
Open the competition in the revision app (link entries), category Silver, closing three weeks after launch (avoid mock week).
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch with a 90-second example you made yourself (or a good one from a reputable site) and discuss what works.
Pupils plan using a three-part storyboard: hook, explanation, example.
Lunchtime recording space with headsets for pupils without a quiet place at home.
Remind pupils to check sharing settings so the teacher can open the link.
Close entries and watch at 1x speed to judge.
resources: PowerPoint recording or other school-approved tool

rubric.look: Top marks: correct and complete for GCSE level, correct terminology. Low marks: errors or oversimplified.
Top marks: a Year 11 would understand it first time; good example or analogy. Low marks: confusing.
Top marks: clear audio, readable visuals, smooth pace. Low marks: hard to hear or read.
Top marks: 90 seconds or under, no faces, sources credited. Low marks: over time or rules broken.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden (pupils must not show names in the video). A People's Choice is voted by Year 11 pupils after watching the top eight. Tie-break on Accuracy. About 40 entries take around 90 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Add the best explainers to the revision web app as revision videos (with permission).
Screen the winners at a lunchtime 'film festival'.
Play the winner in Year 11 and 12 assemblies.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: GCSE Unit 1 networks, cloud, cyber security and legislation; digital applications (multimedia).
comps.extension: Write five multiple-choice questions to go with your video for the revision app.
comps.safety: No faces, full names, uniforms with names, or other pupils in recordings. Share only within the school. Copyright-free music and images only, credited.

comps.title: One-Slide Wonder Revision Cards
comps.summary: Year 12 make one high-quality revision card on a GCSE topic, as a quick, low-pressure task before the exams.
comps.brief: Before the exams, help everyone revise by designing one perfect revision card. Pick a topic from Unit 1 or Unit 4 and fit the key facts, a diagram and one exam tip onto a single slide. It should be accurate, easy to remember and quick to read. The best cards could be added to the revision app for next year's pupils.

entry.help: Make your card on one PowerPoint or Google Slides slide. Export it as PNG and upload it in the revision app. Do not put your name on the card. One entry per pupil.

setup: Run this just after Easter, before study leave and the main exam season.
Post a topic list on Google Classroom and ask pupils to choose different topics.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Bronze, closing one week after launch.
run: Launch in the last minutes of a revision lesson with one example card.
Remind pupils it should be quick: about 45 minutes.
Pupils without home access can make it in a lunchtime session.
Close after one week and judge in one sitting.

rubric.look: Top marks: every fact correct and exam-relevant. Low marks: errors.
Top marks: diagram, mnemonic or example that sticks. Low marks: just a wall of text.
Top marks: clear, readable, uncluttered. Low marks: hard to read.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden. Tie-break on Accuracy. About 50 entries take around 45 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Bronze (1st 20, 2nd 15, 3rd 10, 4th 5) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Add the winning cards to the revision web app for next year (with permission).
Print a set of the best cards for the DT room wall.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: GCSE Unit 1 and Unit 4 revision across all topics.
comps.extension: Make a set of three cards that link together, for example on all three types of test data.
comps.safety: Own wording and diagrams; do not copy from textbooks or revision websites.

comps.title: Class Act: OOP Design Challenge
comps.summary: Year 13 design and code a C# class hierarchy for a house sports system using inheritance, encapsulation and polymorphism.
comps.brief: ERGS needs a system to record events and results for the houses. Design a class hierarchy in C# with a base class (for example Event) and at least two subclasses (for example TrackEvent and FieldEvent), plus a House class that stores points. Use encapsulation with properties, inheritance, and at least one overridden method that behaves differently in each subclass. Include a class diagram and a short Main program that demonstrates it. Great entries are well designed, correctly use OOP principles and are clearly documented.

entry.help: Put your C# code files and a class diagram image in a folder in your school OneDrive (or a GitHub repository if you already have an account and are 13 or over). Share it as 'People in Enniskillen Royal Grammar School with the link can view' or make the repository public, and paste the link in the revision app. Do not include your name in the code comments. One entry per pupil.

setup: Write a short specification and post it on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (link entries), category Silver, closing three weeks after launch.
Prepare a model class diagram notation reminder.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch at the end of an OOP lesson by discussing which classes and attributes the system needs.
Mid-point check in a lesson: pupils share class diagrams and give peer feedback.
Lunchtime support for compiler errors.
Reminder to test sharing links before submitting.
Close and run each Main program to judge.
resources: Visual Studio or school C# environment

rubric.look: Top marks: sensible classes, correct inheritance, good encapsulation. Low marks: everything in one class.
Top marks: overridden methods used meaningfully through a base-class reference. Low marks: none.
Top marks: accurate diagram with attributes, methods, access modifiers and relationships. Low marks: missing or inaccurate.
Top marks: compiles, runs, well commented, Main shows all features. Low marks: does not compile.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden. Tie-break on OOP design. About 15 entries take around an hour. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Present the winning design to Year 12 as a 'what A level programming looks like' example.
Display the winning class diagram in the DT room.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: A level OOP in C# (classes, objects, inheritance, encapsulation, polymorphism), systems development (design).
comps.extension: Add an interface (for example IScorable) and a collection that sorts houses by points.
comps.safety: Use made-up pupil data only. Credit any code adapted from elsewhere.

comps.title: SQL Sleuth: The Missing Trophy
comps.summary: Year 13 solve a fictional mystery by writing SQL queries against a teacher-made school database.
comps.brief: The inter-house trophy has vanished from the display cabinet! You are given a fictional database containing tables for visitors, door access logs, staff rotas and CCTV notes. Write SQL queries using SELECT, WHERE, JOINs, ORDER BY and aggregate functions to narrow down the suspects and find the culprit. Submit your queries in order with a one-line explanation of what each told you. The best entries reach the right answer with efficient, well-written queries.

entry.help: Download the database file from Google Classroom and open it in DB Browser for SQLite (installed in school; free to download at home) or the school's database software. Paste each query you used, in order, with a comment line explaining what it showed, then the name of the culprit at the end. Paste everything into the revision app. One entry per pupil or pair.

setup: Build a small fictional SQLite database (4 tables, about 50 rows each) with a single logical culprit; all names invented.
Write the story intro and post it with the database file on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (text entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch in a databases lesson: read the story and run the first query together.
Give a hint sheet on JOIN syntax rather than hints about the answer.
Lunchtime sessions on school PCs with DB Browser installed.
Reminder three days before close.
Close and check queries for correctness and efficiency.
resources: DB Browser for SQLite (free) on school PCs

rubric.look: 10 for the correct culprit with supporting queries, 0 for a wrong or unsupported answer.
Top marks: queries are correct and use JOINs, WHERE and aggregates appropriately. Low marks: errors or brute force.
Top marks: each step explained, showing logical deduction. Low marks: no explanation.
Top marks: few, well-targeted queries. Low marks: many repetitive queries.

comps.judging: Teacher marks with names hidden. Tie-break on earliest submission time. About 15 entries take around 45 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Reveal the culprit in an A level lesson with the winners' queries.
Offer the mystery as a challenge for GCSE pupils on the department website.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: A level databases and SQL (SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, aggregate functions), data representation.
comps.extension: Design and normalise a new table for the database and write a mystery of your own.
comps.safety: All names and data must be fictional; do not use real staff or pupil names.

comps.title: Post-Exam Web App Build Day
comps.summary: After AS exams, Year 13 house teams build a small web app that solves a school problem in one day.
comps.brief: Your exams are over, so it is time to build something. In house teams, design and build a small web app that solves a real school problem, such as a lost property board, a club finder or a revision timer. It should use HTML, CSS and JavaScript, store some data (for example in localStorage), and work on a phone screen. Great entries solve a real problem, work reliably, are easy to use and show good teamwork.

entry.help: Put your project files in a shared school OneDrive folder (or a GitHub repository with GitHub Pages if team members are 13 or over and already have accounts). Share it as 'People in Enniskillen Royal Grammar School with the link can view', and paste the link in the revision app. Include a README text file explaining what the app does and who did what. One entry per team.

comps.time: 1 day (or 3 lessons) after AS exams in late June
setup: Book the DT room for one day after AS exams finish.
Prepare a list of school problems as ideas, and a simple HTML, CSS and JavaScript starter.
Open the competition in the revision app (link entries), category Silver, closing at the end of the build day.
Ask pupils to form house teams in advance.
run: Start with a 30-minute planning session: user stories and a sketch.
Build in the morning; quick stand-up before lunch.
Afternoon: test with another team as users and fix issues.
Final 30 minutes: each team gives a 3-minute demo.
Submit links by the end of the day.
resources: School PCs with a code editor and browser

rubric.look: Top marks: clear user need met well. Low marks: no clear purpose.
Top marks: JavaScript logic works, data stored, responsive layout. Low marks: static page only.
Top marks: easy to use, accessible contrast and labels. Low marks: confusing.
Top marks: clear demo, everyone contributed. Low marks: one person did everything.

comps.judging: Teacher and a guest judge (another staff member or Year 14 leaver) score demos and code; names are not needed, only house team names. Tie-break on Solves a real problem. About 4 to 6 teams take around an hour. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Showcase the winning app at the end-of-year Digital Technology celebration.
Host the winning app on the department site if it is safe and useful.
Certificates for team members.
comps.curriculum: A level web applications (client-side scripting, HTML, CSS, JavaScript), systems development, user-centred design.
comps.extension: Add a back end or plan how the app would scale securely to the whole school.
comps.safety: No real pupil data or logins; use made-up data. Apps must not collect personal information.

comps.title: AI on Trial: Op-Ed Challenge
comps.summary: Year 14 write a 600-word opinion piece on an AI ethics question, using legislation and technical understanding.
comps.brief: Should AI be allowed to mark exams, choose who gets a job, or decide prison sentences? Choose one question from the list and write a 600-word opinion piece for a newspaper audience. You must explain how the AI works at a suitable level, consider both sides, refer to relevant legislation (such as UK GDPR or the Data Protection Act 2018) and reach a clear conclusion. The best pieces are well argued, accurate and persuasive without exaggerating.

entry.help: Write your piece in Word or Google Docs, check the word count (500 to 650 words), and paste the text into the revision app. Include a short list of sources at the end. Do not include your name. One entry per pupil.

setup: Post a list of four AI ethics questions on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (text entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
Prepare a short guide on op-ed structure.
run: Launch with a 15-minute class debate on one of the questions.
Remind pupils to link to the A level spec: AI, legislation, ethics.
Offer optional feedback on a plan (not a full draft).
Reminder three days before close.
Judge within a week.

rubric.look: Top marks: AI explained correctly, for example training data, bias and how predictions are made. Low marks: errors.
Top marks: both sides considered, clear conclusion, well reasoned. Low marks: one-sided or no conclusion.
Top marks: relevant laws and ethical principles applied correctly. Low marks: none mentioned.
Top marks: engaging, well structured, correct spelling and grammar. Low marks: hard to follow.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden; invite an English or RE teacher as a guest judge. Tie-break on Argument. About 12 entries take about an hour. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Publish the winning piece in the school newsletter or website (no full name, with permission).
Share with Year 13 as an exemplar for extended answers.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: A level AI, legislation (data protection, computer misuse), ethics and impact of digital technology.
comps.extension: Turn the piece into a 5-minute debate at a lunchtime Digital Technology society meeting.
comps.safety: Your own words only; any AI tool use must be declared, and AI-written text will not earn marks. Credit all sources.

comps.title: Secure by Design: Find the Flaws
comps.summary: Year 14 review a paper design of an insecure school web app, identify vulnerabilities and propose fixes.
comps.brief: A developer has designed a school club sign-up web app with lots of security flaws. You are given the design: login page, database table, sample code and network diagram, all on paper. Find as many vulnerabilities as you can (for example SQL injection, passwords stored in plain text, no HTTPS, weak validation) and explain the risk and a fix for each. The best entries find the most real flaws, rank them by risk and give technically correct fixes.

entry.help: Read the design pack from Google Classroom. Write a table or list: flaw, where it is, risk, fix. Paste it into the revision app. Do not test anything on real websites or school systems: this is a paper review only. One entry per pupil.

setup: Create a fictional design pack with around 10 deliberate flaws and an answer key.
Post it on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (text entries), category Silver, closing two weeks after launch.
run: Launch in a security lesson by finding one flaw together.
Remind pupils about the Computer Misuse Act and why the review is paper only.
Lunchtime support for anyone who wants to discuss concepts.
Reminder three days before close.
Go through the full answer key in a lesson after judging.

rubric.look: 1 mark per correct flaw, up to 10.
Top marks: impact clearly and correctly explained for each flaw. Low marks: vague.
Top marks: specific, correct fixes such as parameterised queries, hashing with salt, HTTPS. Low marks: generic advice.
Top marks: flaws ranked sensibly by risk with reasoning. Low marks: no ranking.

comps.judging: Teacher marks against the answer key with names hidden. Tie-break on Fixes. About 12 entries take about 45 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Silver (1st 40, 2nd 30, 3rd 20, 4th 10) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Share the winning review with Year 13 as an exemplar.
Use the design pack as revision material.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: A level security (threats, vulnerabilities, encryption, authentication, validation), web applications, legislation (Computer Misuse Act).
comps.extension: Rewrite the vulnerable code securely in C# with parameterised queries and password hashing.
comps.safety: Paper-based review only. No attempts to test or exploit real websites or school systems; that would break the Computer Misuse Act 1990.

comps.title: Legacy Byte
comps.summary: Year 14 leave a short revision tip or 'what I wish I'd known' message for next year's GCSE and A level pupils.
comps.brief: Before you leave ERGS, share your wisdom. Write a short piece (100 to 200 words) for future Digital Technology pupils: your best revision tip, a topic you finally understood and how, or what you wish you had known at the start. The best entries are honest, specific and genuinely useful.

entry.help: Type your message straight into the revision app text box (100 to 200 words). Do not include your full name. One entry per pupil.

setup: Run this just after Easter, before study leave.
Open the competition in the revision app (text entries), category Bronze, closing one week after launch.
Post one example message on Google Classroom.
run: Launch at the end of a revision lesson.
Remind pupils it should only take 20 minutes.
Pupils on study leave or absent can submit from home through the app before the closing date.
Close after one week and judge in one sitting.

rubric.look: Top marks: specific, practical advice that a pupil could act on. Low marks: vague.
Top marks: real experience shared thoughtfully. Low marks: generic.
Top marks: clear and well written. Low marks: hard to follow.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden. Tie-break on Usefulness. About 12 entries take about 20 minutes. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Bronze (1st 20, 2nd 15, 3rd 10, 4th 5) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Add the winning messages to the revision app as 'Advice from Year 14'.
Display on the DT room wall for next year.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: A level and GCSE revision skills; reflection on the course.
comps.extension: Record a short faceless audio version for the revision app.
comps.safety: No personal information about other pupils or staff.

comps.title: Safer Internet Day Challenge
comps.summary: Whole-school poster or infographic for Safer Internet Day (Tuesday 9 February 2027) on that year's official theme.
comps.brief: Safer Internet Day is on Tuesday 9 February 2027. Create a poster or infographic that helps pupils at ERGS stay safe and kind online, based on this year's official theme. Year 8 and 9 should focus on clear, practical advice; Years 10 to 14 should include a fact, statistic or real-world example. The best entries are eye-catching, accurate and make people stop and think.

entry.help: Make your poster in PowerPoint, Google Slides or Canva for Education (if your class has been invited by a teacher). Export it as PNG and upload it in the revision app. Use only your own images or free-to-use ones, and credit them. Do not put your name or any photos of people on the poster. One entry per pupil.

comps.time: 3 weeks (late January to Safer Internet Day)
setup: Check the UK Safer Internet Centre website for this year's theme and resources.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Platinum, closing the Friday before Safer Internet Day.
Announce in whole-school assembly in late January.
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch with the official Safer Internet Day assembly or lesson resources.
KS3 classes can make posters in a lesson; older years as homework.
Lunchtime sessions for pupils without home access.
Remind form teachers to encourage entries.
Close the Friday before Safer Internet Day; judge over the weekend.
Announce winners on Safer Internet Day itself.
resources: PowerPoint, Google Slides or Canva for Education

rubric.look: Top marks: clear, correct, useful advice linked to the theme. Low marks: vague or inaccurate.
Top marks: eye-catching, readable, well laid out. Low marks: cluttered.
Top marks: suits the intended age group. Low marks: wrong level.
Top marks: fresh idea or approach. Low marks: generic slogans.

comps.judging: Teacher and two sixth-form digital prefects judge with names hidden, in KS3 and KS4/5 categories, then choose overall 1st to 4th. A People's Choice by pupil vote runs separately. Tie-break on Message. About 150 entries take around 3 hours across judges. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Platinum (1st 200, 2nd 150, 3rd 100, 4th 50) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Whole-school corridor display on Safer Internet Day.
Winning posters shown in assembly and on screens around school.
Share on school social media with permission (no names or faces).
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: Y8 Online Safety, Y10 E-Safety, GCSE Unit 1 cyber security and legal and ethical issues; TransformED E1, E4, C5.
comps.extension: Create a short video or podcast version of your poster for the school website.
comps.safety: No photos of people. Canva is for 13 and over unless used through Canva for Education with a teacher's class. Credit all images.

comps.title: Festive Code Week
comps.summary: An Hour of Code style challenge in December with tiered festive coding tasks for every year group.
comps.brief: It is Computer Science Education Week in early December, so it is time to code something festive. Choose the challenge for your level: KS3 can make a festive Scratch animation or micro:bit light show; GCSE and A level can write a C# program such as a gift budget planner, a snowflake drawing or a festive quiz. Your code should be original, work correctly and make people smile. The best entries are creative, well coded and suitable for their level.

entry.help: Scratch or MakeCode: share your project and paste the link. C#: put your code in your school OneDrive, share it within ERGS, and paste the link. Do not include your name in the project. One entry per pupil or pair.

setup: Post challenge sheets for each level on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (link entries), category Gold, closing at the end of the week.
Announce in assembly at the start of December.
Book the DT room every lunchtime that week.
run: Run an Hour of Code style lesson for KS3 classes.
Daily lunchtime coding club with festive music.
Share one 'entry of the day' screenshot to build excitement.
Close at the end of the week; judge before the Christmas holidays.

rubric.look: Top marks: original, fun, festive idea. Low marks: copied or minimal.
Top marks: good use of concepts for the pupil's year group. Low marks: very basic for the level.
Top marks: runs without errors and does what it says. Low marks: broken.

comps.judging: Teacher judges with names hidden in KS3, GCSE and A level groups, then chooses overall 1st to 4th taking level into account. Tie-break on Creativity. About 80 entries take around 3 hours. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Gold (1st 80, 2nd 60, 3rd 40, 4th 20) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Festive lunchtime showcase of the best projects.
Assembly slideshow before Christmas.
Share winners on the school website with permission.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: KS3 Scratch and micro:bits, GCSE Unit 4 C# programming, A level programming; TransformED S1, S3.
comps.extension: Add user input or a scoring system to your project.
comps.safety: Scratch for under 13s via a parent-approved or teacher class account or the offline editor. No names in projects. Own or free-licence assets only.

comps.title: Made by Me: Digital Art with an Honesty Label
comps.summary: Pupils create original digital art and attach an 'honesty label' explaining the tools used and why AI-generated art raises ethical questions.
comps.brief: With AI able to create realistic images in seconds, how do we know what is real and who made it? Create an original piece of digital art (drawing, pixel art, photo edit of your own landscape photo, or vector design) on the theme 'Fermanagh in the future'. Add an honesty label of 50 to 100 words saying which tools you used, how you made it, and one reason why labelling AI-generated images matters. The best entries are creative, skilful and thoughtful about the ethics.

entry.help: Create your artwork in any tool you have used in class, for example Piskel, Google Drawings, PowerPoint or a photo editor. Do not use AI image generators for your entry. Put the artwork and your honesty label on one slide, export it as PNG, and upload it in the revision app. No photos of people. One entry per pupil.

setup: Post the brief and a sample honesty label on Google Classroom.
Open the competition in the revision app (image entries), category Gold, closing three weeks after launch.
Announce in assemblies for eligible years (not Years 12 and 14 because of exams).
Book the DT room for two lunchtimes a week during the competition so pupils without a computer or kit at home can work on school machines.
run: Launch with a 'real or AI?' quiz of five images in assembly or lessons.
Discuss copyright and ownership of AI-generated content.
Lunchtime art and tech sessions.
Reminder three days before close.
Judge within a week.

rubric.look: Top marks: skilful, striking, fits the theme. Low marks: rushed.
Top marks: clearly own work and creative idea. Low marks: derivative or copied.
Top marks: clear explanation of tools and a thoughtful ethical point. Low marks: missing or shallow.

comps.judging: Teacher and an Art teacher judge with names hidden; separate KS3 and KS4/5 shortlists, then overall 1st to 4th. Tie-break on Originality. About 80 entries take around 2 hours. Award 1st to 4th plus Highly commended. House points: every valid entry earns 1 point for its house; places 1st to 4th earn Gold (1st 80, 2nd 60, 3rd 40, 4th 20) house points, announced at launch. Highly commended gets a certificate but no extra points.
display: Exhibition in the library or corridor.
Share on school social media with permission.
Assembly slideshow.
Certificates for placed entries.
comps.curriculum: Y9 Computer Graphics, digital ethics, GCSE Unit 1 ethics and law, A level legislation; TransformED E1, E3, E4.
comps.extension: Write a short guide for younger pupils on how to spot AI-generated images.
comps.safety: No AI-generated entries. No photos of people. Credit any free-licence assets.
